note: The canto opens still in the ninth ditch, among the sowers of discord of Canto 28, who are slashed open by a devil's sword.

context: He hurries Dante on, as he will again at the end of Canto 30. Twice in these cantos Dante lingers over a sight and is told to move.

note: One of the very few measurements given in Hell. The next ditch is said to be eleven miles around (Inferno 30). Readers have long tried to work out the size of the whole pit from these figures, without agreement.

quote: the moon is already beneath our feet
note: The moon is on the far side of the earth, straight below them. It was full two nights before, so the sun is now nearly overhead: early afternoon on the Saturday before Easter. Time in Hell is always told by the moon and stars, never by the sun.
The whole journey through Hell takes about a day, from Friday evening to Saturday evening. Only a few hours remain.

quote: a spirit of my own blood
note: A kinsman of Dante's among the sowers of discord. The poet puts a member of his own family in Hell, and makes himself slow to leave him.

A first cousin of Dante's father. The records show a quarrelsome man, and early commentators say he was killed by one of the Sacchetti family of Florence. Some of them add that his nephews took revenge about thirty years later.

quote: the one who once ruled Altaforte
context: Altaforte is Hautefort, Bertran's castle. He was the headless figure holding up his own head at the end of Canto 28.

note: In Dante's Florence a murdered man's kin were expected to avenge him, and the law allowed for it. In 1300 no one had avenged Geri. Dante feels the family's shame and pities him. Virgil simply tells him to think of other things, and the poem leaves the two views side by side.
The tenth and last ditch. Dante calls it a cloister and its sinners "brothers", as if it were a monastery: a bitter joke.

context: The tenth ditch holds the falsifiers, in four kinds: of metals (alchemists), of persons (impersonators), of money (counterfeiters) and of words (liars). All are punished with disease.

note: The valley of the river Chiana, in Tuscany south of Arezzo. In Dante's time it was a marsh, notorious for malaria in the hot months.
The Maremma is the marshy coast of southern Tuscany. Like Sardinia, it was known for its fevers.
In Hell, Dante and Virgil almost always turn to the left as they go down. The left was the side of evil. On the mountain of Purgatory they will turn to the right.

God's justice, pictured as an officer who cannot make a mistake. Dante's Italian says she "registers" the forgers: she writes them down in her book, as a notary would. These sinners falsified records, and the true record now holds them.

An island near Athens. In the myth, Juno sent a plague that killed every living thing on it, because it bore the name of a nymph Jupiter had loved. Its king, Aeacus, prayed to Jupiter, who turned the ants of an oak tree into men to repeople it. They were called Myrmidons, from the Greek word for ant.

context: The story of the plague of Aegina comes from Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book 7. "As the poets tell us" marks it as a tale, set beside what Dante says he truly saw.

note: The two alchemists who will speak: Griffolino of Arezzo and Capocchio. The similes for them come from the kitchen and the stable, in keeping with the low, comic manner of these cantos.
The alchemists suffer a kind of leprosy. They claimed to change base metals into gold and only corrupted them. Now their own bodies are corrupted, and their skin flakes off like a false coating.
Virgil's courtesy is mocking. To win an answer he wishes the soul well in the only way open to it: may it be able to scratch forever.
The world of the living. Dante offers what the damned most often want from him: to be remembered on earth.

context: He does not give his name. The early commentators supply it.

note: Albero, a young Sienese nobleman. Early commentators say he was the son, or the favorite, of the bishop of Siena.

context: To "make him Daedalus" is to teach him to fly. Albero took the joke seriously.

quote: one who treated him like a son
note: The bishop of Siena, who had Griffolino burned at the stake as a heretic to please Albero.

The attempt to turn cheap metals into gold or silver. It is punished here as fraud: passing off a worked-up metal as the real thing. Griffolino was put to death for a charge that was false, and damned for a sin that no court caught.

context: The bishop's court burned Griffolino for the wrong crime. Minos, who cannot be fooled, sent him here for the real one.

note: A Florentine's jab at the rival city. Vain here means empty-headed and showy. Dante mocks Siena's foolish hopes again in Purgatorio 13.
The French had a name in Italy for vanity and love of display.
Every "except" in this speech is sarcasm: each man named was a famous waster of money. Stricca is usually thought to be one of the Salimbeni family of Siena, but his identity is uncertain.

Another rich Sienese, often said to be Stricca's brother. He is credited with some extravagant new way of cooking with cloves, then a very costly spice from the East. What exactly he invented is not known.
Siena, the soil in which such seeds of luxury readily sprout.
The Spendthrift Brigade, a club of rich young Sienese of the later 1200s. According to the early commentators, they pooled a fortune and ran through it in a couple of years of feasting.
A member of the Brigade from Asciano, a town near Siena, who sold off his lands to pay for his share.
A nickname meaning "Dazzled" or "Muddlehead". He is identified as Bartolomeo dei Folcacchieri, who later held public offices in Siena. The praise of his wit is one more sneer.

context: "You must remember" suggests the two had met, as the early commentators say.

note: A skilled imitator. Medieval thought held that art follows nature as a pupil follows a master (Inferno 11). The alchemist only apes it, copying the look of gold without the substance.
